Carthage

The ruins of Carthage on the Gulf of Tunis, in present-day Tunisia.

Carthage was an ancient city in Northern Africa, on the eastern side of the Lake of Tunis in what is now Tunisia. Carthage was one of the most powerful and important trading entities in the Mediterranean from the 6th to the 2nd century BC, and the centre of the Carthaginian civilisation. The city developed from a Phoenician colony founded, according to tradition, by Queen Dido (Elissa) in the late 9th century BC (conventionally 814 BC) into a large and wealthy metropolis — probably the richest city of its era — sustained by maritime trade, agriculture in its fertile hinterland, and colonies and trading posts from Iberia to Sicily and Sardinia.

Civilisation and government

Carthage was ruled as a commercial oligarchic republic, with annually elected magistrates (suffetes) and a powerful senate; Aristotle praised its constitution in the Politics. Its religion centred on Baal Hammon and the goddess Tanit. Carthaginian fleets dominated the western Mediterranean, and its armies — largely mercenary forces led by generals such as Hamilcar Barca and his son Hannibal — projected power across the region.

Punic Wars and destruction

Competition with the Roman Republic produced the three Punic Wars (264–146 BC). In the Second Punic War Hannibal crossed the Alps with war elephants in 218 BC and shattered Roman armies at Cannae (216 BC), but failed to break Rome's alliances; Scipio Africanus finally defeated him at Zama in 202 BC. In the Third Punic War, Rome besieged and utterly destroyed Carthage in 146 BC. A century later Julius Caesar ordered a Roman colony refounded on the site; Roman Carthage became one of the empire's great cities, later a Vandal, Byzantine and finally Arab-held centre before its decline.

The city's long arc — from sea power destroyed by a rival, commemorated like later defeats at Trafalgar — remains a touchstone of Mediterranean history; its archaeological site is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
